Messages.Author: Ben Swainbank
Messages.Body:
Are tournament standings legitimate considerations under the "playing
to win" doctrine? This comes up with some frequency in tournament
finals. Is it perfectly sportsmanlike playing-to-win-play to
orchestrate a table-split (or time-out) in order to tie the game with
someone of lower standings to secure the tournament win? Or are
players obligated to always try to maximize VPs -- with tournament
standings an "out of game consideration"?

How about in a preliminary round? Is it legitimate to consider whether
the success or failure of another player or deck increases or
decreases your chances of winning the tournament itself? And use that
judgment to assist or thwart a player? Or are players obligated to
stick with maximizing VPs regardless of standings or potential finals
match-ups?

-Ben Swainbank

Messages.Author: Curevei
Messages.Body:


My understanding is that tournament position is an out of game consideration
that is not supposed to affect how one plays the games.

In the real world, since the point of a tournament is to win the tournament, I
will do what gives me the best chances of winning the tournament. Doesn't
bother me when others do the same, like trying to get someone ousted because
they don't want to see that deck in the finals, because, uh, it *makes sense*.
A tournament is greater than the sum of its parts.

One of these days. One of these days, the tournament win with no game wins
goal will be fulfilled (more to point out the failings of tracking game win %
rather than a meaningful stat for ranking purposes, but it has these side
benefits).

On 1 Mar 2004 11:16:24 -0800, bswai...@hotmail.com (Ben Swainbank)
scrawled:

>Are tournament standings legitimate considerations under the "playing
>to win" doctrine?

'Playing to win' doctrine states you must play to win _the current
game_, and applies to all rounds of a tournament including the final.
win == strictly more vps than anyone else.
if you can't 'reasonably' expect to win you must play to get as many
more vps as you can.
if you can't 'reasonably' expect to gain any more vps, you can gain
those 0 vps however you want.

'reasonably' seems to be something you need to be able to convince the
judge of.

Yeah. There seems to be a serious theory and practice split here.
Players who "secretly" play conservatively or split tables in order to
win tournaments seems to engaging in a rather common practice. And its
hard to say that this is unsportsmanlike conduct. You've showed up a
card tournament and you're trying to win it. What's the problem?

Isn't this accepted pactice in other games. In a multi-game Chess
match up isn't it common for the guy who gets the lead to play for the
draws thereafter -- force the guy who's behind to make something
happen.

This seems like reality already. As a prominent example I would site
Jared Strait's 2002 NAC win, which is interesting in that it was high
profile and LSJ was officiating. In the finals, Jared was ousted his
prey and then later ousted his new prey and sad new cross-table
grand-prey simulataniously. Jared had 2 VP and was higher seed than
the one remaining player (who had 0 VP). So, he conceded to his
predator and won the tournament. But the GAME was tied 2-2-1.

Was that unsportsman-like play? Should they have been forced to play
it out even though Jared couldn't possibly not win the tournament?

In the finals at least, its seems like players who are trying to win
the tournament are clearly "playing to win", that tournament standings
DO and should impact players in-game stragegies, and that sanctioning
this behavior would just be accepting something good players are
already covertly doing already - because they are trying to win.

-Ben Swainbank

LSJ wrote:

> In the preliminary rounds, "winning the game" is "get a Game Win".
> In the final, "winning the game" is "winning the final."

Having a single, unified standard is more appealing. I think it would
be better to retain the "Game Win" criteria of the qualifying rounds,
discard the win-by-seeding rule, and let timed out finals resolve with
no winner; roll the prize support over for the next turn, and maybe 2x
the goodies will be an incentive to *play* rather than muse. The number
of non-resolved finals may also increase attention to how many of them
just don't finish.
